chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
title: The happy McShann band and 'The Master's in His Solitude'
summary: McShann created a family atmosphere and a half-finished tune that gave rise to the flatted fifth.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But I see a lot of variety in his playing. But in those days back there, McShann was really cooking. And I'd say he was as much an influence on Bird as the other guys who had supposedly taught him, and all that kind of stuff. First of all, McShann, by his own personality, created as a happy band. The guys were like family, and in fact, like I said, I'd pick up all the guys, go to work, and we'd all get in the car and go back home. Then we'd go in some restaurant, or some place in town. And it was like a happy family. You knew he was the boss, but you still -- you could sit down and talk with him and cuss him out, or whatever, you know. It was a real good feeling like that.
So McShann would hit on some particular phrase or something on his piano, you know, and different ones could do it. But McShann was right up there with all of that.

In fact, there's a tune, long before we came to New York, that McShann created; he never finished. And that was, "The Master's in his Solitude," today. You know, he'd get drunk and he'd say, "I'm the master." He'd get half tore up, you know, not drunk. But he'd say, "I'm the master," you know, and he'd play this thing. NOW, that last note (sings) "The Master's in his Solitude," that's where that flatted fifth started coming in. It's just that thing, (humming). And so they were -- he had a lot to do with -- you know.
